--- title: "Maximal vs. Parsimonious Random Effects" --- # Maximal vs. Parsimonious Random Effects ## The Debate In 2013, Barr, Levy, Scheepers, & Tily published an influential paper titled "Random Effects Structure for Confirmatory Hypothesis Testing: Keep It Maximal." Their argument: > To control Type I error at the nominal level, researchers should include the *maximal* random effects structure — every random slope that is justified by the experimental design. In a within-subjects design where every participant sees every condition, you must include a random slope for condition by participants. Omitting this random slope will produce anti-conservative p-values. Two years later, Matuschek, Kliegl, Vasishth, Baayen, & Bates (2017) pushed back in a paper titled "Balancing Type I Error and Power in Linear Mixed Models." Their argument: > Maximal models frequently fail to converge or produce degenerate variance components. Over-parameterized models can actually have *worse* power than well-specified parsimonious models. Use likelihood ratio tests to decide what to include. Both papers are correct. The question is when each applies. ## Why Maximal Models Can Fail ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Simulate a within-subjects design # Each participant sees each condition 4 times (trials) # 40 participants × 3 conditions × 4 trials = 480 observations # Random effects needed: 40 × 3 = 120 — well below 480 n_participants <- 40 n_conditions <- 3 n_trials <- 4 participant_intercepts <- rnorm(n_participants, 50, 8) # Small (but nonzero) random slopes participant_slopes <- rnorm(n_participants, 0, 0.5) df_within <- expand_grid( participant = 1:n_participants, condition = 1:n_conditions, trial = 1:n_trials ) |> mutate( condition_eff = c(-2, 0, 2)[condition], # condition effect p_slope = participant_slopes[participant], Y = participant_intercepts[participant] + condition_eff + p_slope * condition_eff + rnorm(n(), 0, 5), participant = factor(participant), condition = factor(condition) ) # Maximal model m_max <- lmer(Y ~ condition + (condition | participant), data = df_within, control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")) # Does it converge? library(performance) check_convergence(m_max) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE attr(,"gradient") [1] 7.545173e-07 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Parsimonious model (random slope variance is tiny — can drop it) m_pars <- lmer(Y ~ condition + (1 | participant), data = df_within) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Compare: do the p-values differ substantially? anova(m_pars, m_max) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| | npar| AIC| BIC| logLik| -2*log(L)| Chisq| Df| Pr(>Chisq)| |:------|----:|--------:|--------:|---------:|---------:|--------:|--:|----------:| |m_pars | 5| 3045.677| 3066.546| -1517.838| 3035.677| NA| NA| NA| |m_max | 10| 3041.815| 3083.553| -1510.907| 3021.815| 13.86175| 5| 0.0165119|
::: ::: ## The Decision Framework The current consensus among methodologists: ::: {.callout-note} ## When to Use Maximal Random Effects 1. **Within-subjects experimental manipulations:** Always include random slopes for within-subjects factors. This is the critical case. Barr et al. (2013) are correct: omitting random slopes for within-subject conditions inflates Type I error. 2. **When theory or pilot data suggests heterogeneous effects:** If you have prior reason to believe the treatment effect varies substantially across participants, include the random slope. 3. **Large samples:** With enough data, complex models converge and the efficiency loss from over-parameterization is small. ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## When to Simplify (Parsimonious) 1. **Convergence failures:** If the maximal model does not converge, you must simplify. Start by removing the correlation between random intercept and slope (`(1 | participant) + (0 + condition | participant)`). Then consider removing the random slope itself. 2. **Degenerate variance components:** If the random slope variance is estimated at exactly zero (or very near), it is contributing nothing and can be dropped. 3. **Very small variance components:** Use an LRT to test whether the random slope significantly improves fit. If not, the parsimonious model is appropriate. ::: ## A Practical Simplification Protocol ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Step 1: Try the maximal model m_max_2 <- tryCatch( lmer(Y ~ condition + (condition | participant), data = df_within, control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")), warning = function(w) { cat("Warning:", conditionMessage(w), "\n"); NULL } ) # Step 2: If it fails/has issues, remove correlation first m_no_corr <- lmer(Y ~ condition + (1 | participant) + (0 + condition | participant), data = df_within) # Step 3: Test: does the random slope improve fit? anova(m_pars, m_no_corr) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| | npar| AIC| BIC| logLik| -2*log(L)| Chisq| Df| Pr(>Chisq)| |:---------|----:|--------:|--------:|---------:|---------:|--------:|--:|----------:| |m_pars | 5| 3045.677| 3066.546| -1517.838| 3035.677| NA| NA| NA| |m_no_corr | 11| 3043.815| 3089.727| -1510.907| 3021.815| 13.86175| 6| 0.0312192|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} # If p > 0.05 on the LRT, the random slope does not help — use m_pars ``` ::: ::: {.callout-warning icon=false} ## Assumption: The Random Effects Structure Matches the Design **What it means:** The random effects you include should reflect the actual nesting structure of your design. A random slope for a between-subjects factor makes no statistical sense (between-subjects factors cannot vary within a subject). **Common mistake:** Including a random slope for a between-subjects condition. This will either produce a degenerate model or absorb all variance in a nonsensical way. **How to check:** For each predictor, ask: does this variable vary *within* the grouping unit (participant, stimulus)? If yes, it can have a random slope for that unit. If no (between-subjects), it cannot. :::
